1. Accidental Release Prevention and Emergency Response Policies
SEMCO South Cooling facility conducts inspection procedures to review refrigeration equipment prior to startup and during operations. These procedures identify potential sources of release and equipment corrections required to prevent these releases. On-site personnel and certified refrigeration contractors review the equipment as required. On-site personnel provide initial emergency response.
On-site personnel will make a preliminary assessment in the event of a release and will contact refrigeration contractor. No emergency operations will be performed that are beyond the capabilities of the operators or other on-site personnel. Local fire and police departments with mutual aid response will provide emergency response for a major release event. Refrigeration contractors will be on-call to provide emergency response. Emergency response training will be conducted yearly for current employees and as required for new employees. Records will be kept of all training performed at the site for a minimum of five (5) years.

2. Stationary Source and Regulated Substances Handled
SEMCO South Cooling uses anhydrous ammonia as a refrigerant in their operations. The ammonia system is used for cold storage, vacuum cooling, pressure cooling and ice making operations. There are four (4) interconnected refrigeration systems at the facility. These processes are (1) Fixed System and cold room storage, (4) 12-Palette Half Car Vacuum Cooling Systems, (3) Pressure Cooling Systems (in the cold rooms), and Ice making systems. All refrigeration systems are connected to each other, and the total ammonia quantity is above federal threshold quantity which is approximately 20,322 lb. 
This is a single stage closed loop ammonia refrigeration system. This system operates between 17° F/30 psig on the suction side and 85° F/152 psig on the discharge side during normal operations, and -17° F/5 psig on the suction side and 85° F/152 psi

g on the discharge side during ice making operations. 
Fixed System: The largest system is the Fixed System that serves the Cold Room, and the Pressure Cooler Room. Fixed System is composed of fixed and portable equipment. Fixed equipment includes high- and low-pressure receivers, screw compressors, cold room evaporators, evaporative condenser, ammonia pumps, ammonia detection, control systems, and diffusion tank. Portable equipment includes four 12-Palette (Half Car) Vacuum Tubes, one Refrigeration Trailer (R-1112) that is connected to the Fixed System. Fixed System is operated seasonally from November to April. 
Portable Systems: Portable systems include trailer, vacuum tubes, and ice maker. The Refrigeration Trailer (R-1112) consists of two screw compressors, high- and low-pressure receivers, ammonia pumps and the two evaporative condensers. Vacuum Cooling System is composed of four 12-Palette (Half Car) Vacuum Tubes (T-85, T-86, T112, T117). T85 and T-86 vacuum tubes have their own surge drums. T1112 and T1117 do not have surge drums and fed by the ammonia pumps of the LPR-1 vessel. Also, the ice maker does not have a surge drum, and fed by the ammonia pumps of the LPR-1 vessel. Portable System is operated seasonally from November to April. At the end of the season, portable equipment ships to Salinas, CA facility for summer operations, from April to November. 
The facility pumps down all the ammonia in the system to the high-pressure and low-pressure receivers during the off season. 
All the equipment except for coils and pressure coolers are located outdoors.
Refrigeration drawings that shows P&IDs, refrigeration equipment and piping layout are located in the Chapter 8 Appendix 8.1 (Refrigeration System Drawings) of the RMP Binder. A list of refrigeration equipment used at this facility can be found in Appendix 12 of the RMP Binder. International Institute of Ammonia Refrigeration (IIAR) "Ammonia Refrigeration Safety Inspection Checklists," located in Appendix

12 of the RMP Binder, describe equipment details.
Anhydrous ammonia (NH3) is a gas in its natural state and is extremely irritating to mucous membranes and lung tissue. The gas is pungent and may be suffocating as shortness of breath and labored breathing can develop if inhaled. Prolonged inhalation of high concentrations may cause bronchitis and/ or pneumonia, with some residual reduction in pulmonary functions. Repeated or prolonged contact of high concentrations of ammonia to the skin can cause frostbite, redness, pain and serious skin burn. See Chapter 8 Appendix 8.4 for Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for anhydrous ammonia.

3. General Accidental Release Prevention Program
SEMCO South Cooling facility maintains a release prevention program to prevent or mitigate releases. The program includes regular inspections, monitoring equipment and logging conditions, scheduled maintenance, and operator training. There is a program to analyze releases for ways to prevent a similar future release, see Appendix 16 - Incident Investigation of the RMP Binder.
The ammonia refrigeration system has specific safety procedures to prevent a release. All compressors have safety switches that would shut down the compressors upon detection of unsafe operating conditions. Pressure vessels have float switches that control the liquid levels in the vessels. All pressure vessels and compressors are protected against high-pressure situations by safety relief valves, which are tied to an ammonia diffusion tank to prevent high-pressure release to the ambient. All cold rooms are monitored by an ammonia detection system for unsafe ammonia concentration levels. There are assigned responders (refrigeration contractors) experienced with ammonia refrigeration that would respond to and determine specific actions for any incident.

4. Five-Year Accident History
SEMCO South Cooling had no releases of anhydrous ammonia in the last 5 years that resulted in deaths, injuries, or significant property damage on s

ite, or known offsite deaths, injuries, evacuations, sheltering in place, property damage, or environmental damage.

5. Emergency Response Program
SEMCO South Cooling facility is a "Non-Responding" facility. Facility only responds to situations that are within their capabilities. No emergency response actions or site clean-up that are beyond the capabilities of the refrigeration personnel will be performed. In case of an emergency, incident will be reported immediately to the Emergency Coordinator and Refrigeration Contractor. The Emergency Coordinator is responsible for assisting county emergency responders upon arrival on site. This may include contacting emergency response agencies, schools, daycare centers, and acute care facilities that may be affected by the release. The Emergency Coordinator will also be responsible for evacuation of employees if necessary and for coordination with community emergency responders if off-site evacuations are required.

6. Planned Changes to Improve Safety
Recommended corrective actions to mitigate the potential for an accidental ammonia release are proposed on the tables located in RMP Binder Chapter 0.0. The table items result from recommendations made during the Process Hazard Analysis, a Code Compliance Review, Seismic Review, Relief System Design Analysis and a Safety Inspection performed by a qualified person. Some recommendation items in the recommendation table originate from multiple codes but are listed only once. Specific facility areas and systems categorize recommendations resulting from the Safety Inspection; some of which may repeat general Process Hazard Analysis and Code Compliance Review items. 
Based on the severity of the hazards identified, implementation deadlines are also recommended. All refrigeration equipment is well maintained and operated in a safe manner by trained personnel. Operating, maintenance, training, and safety procedures will be formalized with improved written documentation.
